scenes.title: The Definition of Tragedy
scenes.summary: Tragedy is the imitation of a serious, complete action of some magnitude, in embellished language, enacted and not narrated, accomplishing through pity and fear the catharsis of such feelings.

scenes.title: The Six Parts
scenes.summary: From the manner come spectacle, from the media song and diction, from the action plot, character and thought: six parts in all, and every play has them.

scenes.title: Plot First
scenes.summary: The structure of the incidents is the most important: tragedy imitates action and life, not people; there can be tragedy without character, as Zeuxis' painting lacks it, but not without action.

scenes.title: The Soul of Tragedy
scenes.summary: Reversals and recognitions, the strongest means, are parts of the plot; beginners master diction and character first. The plot is the first principle and soul of tragedy, as an outline in white surpasses colors smeared at random.

scenes.title: Thought, Diction, Song, Spectacle
scenes.summary: Thought is saying what fits, as in politics and rhetoric; character reveals choice; diction is expression in words; song is the greatest of the embellishments; spectacle moves us but is the least artistic.
